## Why it matters

Messy text rarely arrives in one exact form. Phone numbers come as `215-555-0134` and as `(215) 555 0134`, and dates, order numbers and email addresses sit inside longer lines of logs, forms and exports.[@pvg-regex] Python's `find` and `replace` need the exact text, so cleaning that kind of data with them turns into loops full of conditions.

A regular expression describes the shape of the text instead, such as four digits in a row or a word at the start of a line, and Python's `re` module finds, extracts, splits or replaces everything that fits.[@pvg-regex] Ask whoever cleans your text data to show the patterns they used, because a pattern that matches more or less than intended changes the data without an error.

## What you will do

The notebook works on short log lines, contact text and a scrap of HTML, and every cell's output is saved in it.[@pvg-regex]

1. Search for a shape with `re.search`, and test the result before using it. A pattern that matches nothing returns `None` instead of raising an error.[@pvg-regex]
2. Write every pattern as a raw string. In an ordinary string `\b` is a backspace, so `re.findall("\bweb", log)` returns an empty list with no warning, while `r"\bweb"` finds the word.[@pvg-regex]
3. Build patterns from `\d`, `\w` and `\s`, your own character classes in square brackets, and counts such as `+` and `{4}`.[@pvg-regex]
4. Pull fields out with named groups, turning a log line that starts `2026-09-04 10:22:31 ERROR` into its date, level and message.[@pvg-regex]
5. Make a greedy pattern lazy. On `<b>bold</b> and <i>italic</i>`, the pattern `<.*>` returns the whole string as one match, and `<.*?>` returns the four tags.[@pvg-regex]
6. Read the three errors the notebook runs on purpose: calling `.group()` on no match, a repeat with nothing in front of it, and a parenthesis that is never closed.[@pvg-regex]

The quickest check of a pattern is the notebook's own. It marks every match inside the original text, so you can see what the pattern caught and what it left alone.[@pvg-regex]

```python
text = "Call 215-555-0134 or 610-555-9876 before 2026-09-04"
print(re.sub(r"\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}", r"[\g<0>]", text))
# Call [215-555-0134] or [610-555-9876] before 2026-09-04
```

[Cleaning is the analysis](../../articles/cleaning-is-the-analysis/index.qmd) finds a genre column typed 19 ways for 8 genres, with spellings that differ in case, spacing and punctuation. Patterns like the ones in this lab are how a column like that is brought back to one spelling per genre.
